reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A chronic, antigen-driven Th2 immune disease of the oesophagus, most common in young atopic men.
Adults present with dysphagia and food bolus impaction; children present with feeding difficulty, vomiting and failure to thrive.
Diagnosis requires symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction plus at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field on biopsy, with other causes excluded.
Take multiple biopsies from proximal and distal oesophagus because involvement is patchy.
Endoscopic features include fixed rings (trachealisation), linear furrows, white exudates, oedema, strictures and crepe-paper mucosa graded by the EREFS score.
Proton pump inhibitor-responsive oesophageal eosinophilia is now regarded as part of the disease spectrum, so proton pump inhibitors are a first-line treatment rather than only a diagnostic filter.
Therapeutic options include proton pump inhibitors, swallowed topical corticosteroids, dietary elimination and endoscopic dilation of strictures.
Untreated inflammation drives fibrostenotic remodelling with progressive strictures and recurrent impaction.
reference.pathophysiology: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic Th2-mediated immune response to food and possibly aeroallergens in genetically predisposed individuals. Antigen exposure triggers release of interleukin-5 and interleukin-13, eosinophil recruitment via eotaxin-3, and mast cell activation, producing an eosinophil-predominant inflammation confined to the oesophagus. Sustained inflammation causes epithelial barrier dysfunction, subepithelial fibrosis and smooth muscle dysfunction, generating the rings, strictures and dysmotility that underlie dysphagia and bolus impaction.
additionalDifferentials: Eosinophilic gastritis or enteritis with oesophageal involvement
Achalasia or other primary oesophageal motility disorder
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with graded (EREFS) assessment
Multiple oesophageal biopsies from proximal and distal levels with eosinophil counts
Treatment trial and histological reassessment on a proton pump inhibitor
Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia
Allergy assessment (skin prick or specific IgE) when dietary therapy is considered
Barium or timed oesophagram to define strictures and calibre
Oesophageal manometry if a motility disorder or achalasia is suspected
redFlags: Acute food bolus impaction requiring emergency endoscopy
Complete dysphagia or inability to manage secretions
Oesophageal perforation after impaction or dilation
Significant weight loss or failure to thrive in children
reference.prognosis: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic relapsing condition that is not life-limiting but tends to recur off treatment; maintenance therapy and surveillance prevent progression to fibrostenotic strictures and recurrent impaction.
pitfalls: Diagnosing on a single biopsy or from one level and missing patchy disease
Failing to treat and reassess, allowing silent progression to strictures
Attributing symptoms solely to reflux and missing the diagnosis
Aggressive dilation without anti-inflammatory therapy, risking mucosal tears
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
International consensus diagnostic criteria for eosinophilic oesophagitis
management: Proton pump inhibitors as first-line therapy to reduce oesophageal eosinophilia and symptoms
Swallowed topical corticosteroids, such as budesonide or fluticasone formulations, as a mainstay of treatment
Dietary elimination therapy, empirical multi-food or allergy-guided, with structured reintroduction to identify triggers
Biologic therapy with dupilumab, targeting IL-4 and IL-13, for refractory disease
Endoscopic dilatation for fibrostenotic strictures causing dysphagia, and emergency endoscopic removal of an impacted food bolus
Maintenance therapy with endoscopic and histological surveillance to prevent fibrostenotic progression
Allergy assessment and dietitian input with gastroenterology follow-up
